course_description:
An introduction to the founding concepts of Art History from the Renaissance to 20th century.

‘Readings in Art History’ examines the methodsﾠ and theories of art historical enquiry. It helps students consider and determine their own approaches to looking at and thinking about art. What kind of art historian/critic/curator are YOU? Course delivery will take the form of a lecture/tutorial series. Students will engage in a dialogue with a number of art historians, theorists and critics and their varying methodological approaches. The course commences with an overview of the origins of art history as a discipline, and proceeds chronologically, concluding with a range of 20th century and contemporary art historical methods. Focusing on primary texts by seminal writers, key concepts such as aesthetics, connoisseurship, iconography, formalism, style, semiotics, structuralism, post-structuralism, postcolonial theory, and globalism, will be discussed. It is essential that students complete each week’s readings prior to the lecture/tutorial, as they will be expected to contribute to the discussion that follows the lecture on the topic.

assessment_details.title: Essay (research/book review)
assessment_details.task_description: For this assessment, you must choose one book from a list that will be distributed via the course Blackboard, and write an critical research essay/book review. Your essay must provide a critical reflection on your chosen book, considering the author's methodology in detail and presenting an argument that contends with the strengths and/or weaknesses of the methodology. Your essay must have a central argument, and must be supported by secondary research (in addition to the consultation of set readings and the recommended reading list, students must source texts independently so as to demonstrate independent research). A separate bibliography must be attached in Chicago style, and references must be done in Chicago notes-bibliography style. Word count does not include footnotes and bibliography, but it does include quotations. Marking criteria and detailed task description will be provided via Blackboard and discussed in lectures + tutorials. While this is officially/technically listed as an 'open' assessment, all students in this course are strongly discouraged from using AI technology in the completion of the essay. This assessment is designed to develop and test your own thinking and writing skills, essential skills in all arts professions. Outsourcing these essential skills to AI technology means that you will not be able to develop these skills over the course of your degree. Read full task description Hide full task description

Week 1 - NO TUTORIALS

Week 2 - Biography and Cultural Approaches to art history Biography vs cultural approaches. This week, we look at classic early art historical texts that use biography as their methodology (Vasari, Van Mander), and compare these to the cultural approach advanced by Winckelmann (often regarded as the 'father of art history'). Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03

Week 2 - Biography and Cultural Approaches to art history Biography vs cultural approaches. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03

Week 3 - aesthetics, Kant and Hegel This week we look at the Enlightenment, and consider two key philosophers: Kant and Hegel. We consider these philosophers' very different approaches to art and aesthetics, and reflect on whether these methods remain relevant to art history today. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03

Week 3 - aesthetics, Kant and Hegel This week we look at the Enlightenment, and consider two key philosophers: Kant and Hegel. We consider these philosophers' very different approaches to art and aesthetics, and reflect on whether these methods remain relevant to art history today. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03

Week 4 - Cultural History versus connoisseurship This week we consider two very different approaches of the 19th century, Jacob Burckhardt's cultural history and Giovanni Morelli's connoisseurship. We place these methodologies in dialogue and consider their respective strengths and weaknesses. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03

Week 4 - Cultural History versus connoisseurship This week we consider two very different approaches of the 19th century, Jacob Burckhardt's cultural history and Giovanni Morelli's connoisseurship. We place these methodologies in dialogue and consider their respective strengths and weaknesses. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03

Week 5 - Iconography, Style, Formalism This week we look at the great institution-builders of the 20th century, a watershed moment for art history as we know it today: Erwin Panofsky and Heinrich Wolfflin. Similar to previous weeks, we compare Panofsky's iconographical method to Wolfflin's formalism, in order to reflect on the strengths and weaknesses of each approach. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03
